title: Ather, iQube, Chetak or Ola S1: Which Electric Scooter Actually Suits a 20 km Bengaluru Commute?
author: Arjun Belavadi
article:
A 20 km daily round trip sounds like the easiest possible brief for an electric scooter. In practice the commute is less about the number on the spec sheet and more about how a scooter copes with the Silk Board crawl, the faster stretches of the Outer Ring Road and the flyovers in between, and what happens on the day something goes wrong. We weighed the four names that dominate most shortlists, the Ather 450, TVS iQube, Bajaj Chetak and Ola S1, on what matters most: reliability, real-world range and the service network behind the badge.

Start with range, because it is the least of your worries. Certified IDC figures come from controlled test cycles, and real-world range in Bengaluru traffic runs well below them thanks to low average speeds, frequent stops and short bursts of acceleration to clear junctions. Even so, 20 km a day is a light load for any of these four, and the larger-battery variants will comfortably go several days between charges.

Speed matters more than first-time buyers expect. Most Bengaluru commutes include at least one arterial stretch, and a top speed of 65 km/h is generally treated as the minimum for keeping pace there. The Ola S1 Pro is in a different league, with 58 Nm and a Vbox-verified top speed of 99.8 km/h against an indicated 115 km/h, and it is the quickest of the four past 60 and 80 km/h. The Ather 450X is the second quickest, topping out at a GPS-rated 80 km/h (90 km/h indicated), and it has the sharpest throttle response of the group. The older Chetak's indicated 69 km/h feels a little stretched on faster roads, though it cleverly switches from Eco to Sport on its own once you twist past half throttle. The TVS iQube is the one that gives us pause: even in Power mode it runs out of breath at an indicated 60 km/h or so, which leaves you being overtaken by buses on the ORR.

Ola's mode tuning also suits the city better than its reputation suggests. Eco mode, which is where most commuters will want to live to stretch range, keeps enough low-speed pull to clear flyovers like Hebbal without fuss, so you rarely need to step up to Normal. The one quirk to get used to is that the S1 Pro cuts power the moment you touch the brakes, which can catch you out during slow U-turns or hill starts; the Chetak does the same, but far more gently.

On comfort, the established makers still lead. The Chetak's wide, well-contoured seat and spot-on rider's triangle are excellent, and the iQube offers the best seat of the four for riding two-up. The Ather is the least comfortable by some margin: a small seat and high-set floorboard make it cramped for riders taller than about 5ft 10in, and its stiff suspension is harsh at low speeds on broken roads. Its consolation is the best handling in the group. The Ola sits in between, with a flat, long seat and a single-sided front fork and monoshock that deal with bumpy roads well, though a spine in the floorboard limits what you can carry at your feet.

Practicality is the Ola's trump card: its 36-litre boot is the largest here. The Ather offers 22 litres, while current iQube variants list 32 litres, although the portable charger eats into that space. The Chetak's boot is shallow, but it is the only one with a glovebox and it has the most compact charger.

That leaves service, the area where Ola has drawn the most criticism. Its much-discussed 2024 service crunch amounted to roughly 8,000 complaints a month across a network of about 430 centres, irritating for the owners caught in it but hardly the collapse social media made it out to be. The company's response, HyperService, set a target of 1,000 service centres by December 2024, a programme to train 100,000 third-party mechanics by 2025, and a one-day resolution guarantee backed by a backup S1 scooter if repairs run longer. TVS and Bajaj, for their part, bring decades of two-wheeler experience and kept their electric sales steady through the same period.

Pricing varies by city and state subsidy, so confirm on-road figures at a showroom. As a guide, the iQube is listed from ₹95,124 to ₹1.30 lakh, the Chetak C35 from ₹1.24 to ₹1.52 lakh, the Ather 450S from ₹1.28 to ₹1.69 lakh and the 450X from ₹1.51 to ₹1.90 lakh.

Our verdict: for a 20 km Bengaluru commute that touches arterial roads, the Ola S1 Pro is the most complete package, combining the strongest performance, the biggest boot and a ride that copes with broken tarmac. The Ather 450X suits riders who value handling above all and can live with a firm ride. The Chetak is the comfort pick for inner-city routes. The iQube is pleasant and well built, but its top speed makes it hard to recommend if your route includes the ORR. Whichever you shortlist, test-ride it on your actual commute before you sign.

falseClaims.truth: Autocar India's test found the iQube S's Eco mode caps speed at 50 km/h while Power mode allows an indicated 80 km/h, enough that it does not feel out of place on faster-flowing roads; 91Wheels lists iQube max speeds of 78-82 km/h across variants.

falseClaims.claim: Eco mode, which is where most commuters will want to live to stretch range, keeps enough low-speed pull to clear flyovers like Hebbal without fuss, so you rarely need to step up to Normal.
falseClaims.truth: Autocar India found the Ola's Eco mode restricts acceleration to a pace that is borderline dangerous in fast-moving city traffic and makes it impossible to climb steep gradients, recommending riders use at least Normal mode; the other three scooters were usable in Eco.

falseClaims.claim: Its much-discussed 2024 service crunch amounted to roughly 8,000 complaints a month across a network of about 430 centres
falseClaims.truth: Ola Electric was receiving an average of about 80,000 service complaints per month, peaking at 6,000-7,000 a day, with many customers waiting 30-45 days for repairs and some service centres holding hundreds of broken-down scooters.
